Unified vs. Specialist YOLO11n Detectors: Failure-Mode Diagnostics on Held-Out Webcam Benchmarks

An empirical failure-mode analysis of unified 36-class versus specialist digit and letter YOLO11n detectors across original and augmented webcam benchmarks, using automated CI benchmark telemetry.

#computer-vision #yolo11 #benchmarking #mlops #ci-cd #error-analysis

Decomposing American Sign Language (ASL) detection into dedicated specialist models can reduce confusion between visually similar hand shapes, such as 0 versus O or 2 versus V, in the robotic swarm-control system (gesture-swarm-ros2).

This analysis compares three YOLO11n detectors:

  • ASL Unified Webcam Gesture Detector
  • ASL Unified Digits Gesture Detector
  • ASL Unified Letters Gesture Detector

The models were evaluated on two published held-out webcam benchmarks:

  • ASL Webcam Benchmark — Original: 36 gesture frames plus 1 background frame.
  • ASL Webcam Benchmark — Augmented: 216 gesture frames plus 6 background frames.

Detection matches require the predicted symbol to equal the ground-truth symbol and the intersection-over-union (IoU) between the predicted and ground-truth bounding boxes to be at least 0.45.

Specialist models are evaluated only against ground-truth annotations within their own class domains. The digit-only model is evaluated against 10 digit annotations in the original benchmark and 60 digit annotations in the augmented benchmark. The letter-only model is evaluated against 26 letter annotations in the original benchmark and 156 letter annotations in the augmented benchmark. Out-of-domain annotations are excluded from the recall denominator and from the missed-class report.

Benchmark telemetry and performance summary

Although all models achieved high precision and mAP@0.50 on their respective validation splits, held-out webcam evaluation revealed a substantial domain gap.

Benchmark Model Evaluation domain In-domain ground truth True positives Recall Background false positives
Original Unified Webcam 0–9, A–Z 36 16 44.44% 0/1
Original Digits Specialist 0–9 10 6 60.00% 0/1
Original Letters Specialist A–Z 26 10 38.46% 0/1
Augmented Unified Webcam 0–9, A–Z 216 50 23.15% 1/6
Augmented Digits Specialist 0–9 60 25 41.67% 0/6
Augmented Letters Specialist A–Z 156 43 27.56% 1/6

The digit-only detector achieved the highest recall on both benchmarks. On the original benchmark, it detected 6 of 10 digit gestures. On the augmented benchmark, it detected 25 of 60 digit instances.

The lower augmented-benchmark results indicate that the current augmentation pipeline is substantially more challenging than the models’ training and validation distributions. Because all augmented variants derive from the same 36 source webcam images, the augmented benchmark measures robustness to controlled transformations rather than providing an independent multi-session estimate of real-world performance.

Failure-mode diagnostics

Background false-positive suppression

Training with negative room frames appears to have suppressed background hallucinations effectively. The digit-only model produced no false positives on either the single original background frame or the six augmented background frames.

The unified and letter-only models each produced one false positive across the six augmented background frames. This is a useful signal that background training helps, but the small number of background images means it should not be treated as a definitive comparison.

A background false positive is defined as a model detection on an image with no ground-truth gesture annotation. Background images are excluded from the recall denominator but remain useful for measuring unwanted detections.

Localization versus classification

Several logged misses were not necessarily symbol misclassifications. In the benchmark telemetry, some predictions assigned the correct symbol but failed the IoU threshold because their bounding boxes were extremely large or poorly localized.

Examples included near-full-frame predictions spanning approximately the entire 640 × 480 image, as well as boxes shifted by aggressive crop transformations. These cases suggest that localization quality, rather than symbol recognition alone, contributed to the benchmark failures.

The conversion pipeline’s fallback boxes are a plausible contributor: when MediaPipe does not provide a reliable hand box, a class- and image-size-aware centered fallback can produce an oversized or poorly positioned box. This hypothesis should be verified by inspecting the affected predictions and their associated fallback source before changing the loss function.

Cross-domain triggering

Running specialist models across the full 36-class benchmark exposed cross-domain triggering. For example, the letter-only model produced high-confidence F predictions on digit frames, while the digit-only model produced predictions on letter frames.

This does not necessarily mean that the specialist models are inherently inferior. It does show that deploying them without an application-level domain gate can create false positives outside their intended recognition context.

For the ROS 2 swarm-control system, specialist detectors should therefore be gated by an explicit interaction state: for example, a numeric-entry state may activate the digit detector, while a command-letter state may activate the letter detector.

Chirality and horizontal flipping

Horizontal flip augmentations appeared to induce severe structural confusions. Observed examples included M being interpreted as A, Z as D, and G as P; digit 2 was also confused with 3, and 4 with 9.

These observations support restricting horizontal flips for asymmetric ASL gestures, where handedness and spatial orientation can alter the visual structure of the sign. Before changing the training configuration, inspect the original and flipped variants for each affected class to separate genuine chirality sensitivity from crop, scale, or localization artifacts.

Earlier manually reported benchmark values may differ from the values in this report if they used a different evaluator version, confidence threshold, matching implementation, or model revision. The values above should therefore be interpreted as the output of this specific reproducible CI evaluation configuration.

Next engineering actions

  1. Restrict horizontal flips for chirality-sensitive gestures. Disable horizontal flips during training and benchmark augmentation for asymmetric ASL signs, or apply them only where handedness is explicitly preserved.

  2. Audit fallback-generated boxes. Inspect predictions with near-full-frame bounding boxes, especially for 1, P, and T, and determine whether MediaPipe failures, Kalman predictions, or centered fallback boxes produced the poor localization.

  3. Evaluate stricter localization matching. Run a sensitivity analysis at IoU thresholds such as 0.30, 0.45, and 0.60 to separate missed detections from poor box regression.

  4. Add ROS 2 mode gating. Use an explicit numeric or command-letter state machine so that specialist detectors receive only images appropriate to their class domain.

  5. Expand the held-out benchmark. Collect multiple original frames per class from separate sessions, lighting conditions, camera positions, and users. This will make per-class recall estimates more stable and allow confidence intervals.

Limitations

  • The original benchmark contains only one image per gesture class.
  • All augmented variants derive from the same 36 source webcam images.
  • The benchmark is therefore not yet a large multi-session held-out test set.
  • The reported results should not be used alone to select a final production model.
  • The augmented benchmark includes transformations that may be more aggressive than the models’ training distribution.
  • Background-image counts are too small to draw strong conclusions about background suppression.
  • The benchmark measures single-frame detection performance; it does not yet evaluate temporal consistency, gesture transitions, or multi-frame tracking.
